triage.name: Hydrocele
triage.reason: Common scrotal swelling that students can diagnose by history and exam (transillumination) with ultrasound to confirm, and distinguish from hernia, varicocele and tumor.

rule_errors: exam: 2 of 5 terms aren't SNOMED CT findings
review_issues: exam: term 'Positive transillumination test' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Tenderness of scrotum' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: Bimodal age distribution: congenital in infants, acquired in men over 40

risk_factors.text: Inguinal hernia or prior hernia repair

chief_complaints.text: It feels heavy or achy down there

hpi.onset: Insidious, or present since birth in congenital cases
hpi.duration: Weeks to months, or lifelong in congenital cases
hpi.progression: Enlarges slowly over time; may fluctuate in size with activity or position if communicating
hpi.location: Scrotum, usually unilateral, surrounding the testicle
hpi.quality: Painless swelling with a heavy, dragging sensation
hpi.timing: Constant swelling; may increase with standing and decrease when lying flat if communicating

associated_symptoms.text: Dull ache or heaviness in the scrotum

pertinent_negatives: Inguinal bulge that disappears when lying down

positives.text: Dull ache or heaviness in the scrotum

atypical.how_it_differs: Usually present at birth as a non-tender scrotal swelling that may change in size with crying or position; can be bilateral and often resolves spontaneously by age 1.
Presents as slowly progressive, painless scrotal enlargement; may go unnoticed until it becomes large and uncomfortable.

general.moderate: Comfortable but may walk with a slightly wide-based gait due to scrotal size; normal vital signs
general.severe: Mild discomfort from heavy scrotal swelling; otherwise well-appearing

findings.finding: Smooth, tense or fluctuant scrotal swelling that may extend upward along the spermatic cord

findings.maneuver: Darken the room and shine a penlight against the side of the scrotal swelling
findings.finding: The entire swelling glows red (positive transillumination)

findings.maneuver: Palpate the testis from the side opposite the swelling, feeling all surfaces
findings.finding: Testis is normal or not separately palpable because surrounded by fluid; no discrete testicular mass

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to cough or bear down while palpating the swelling
findings.finding: No cough impulse felt in the swelling

imaging.preferred_when: First-line imaging for scrotal swelling; non-invasive and widely available

findings.text: Anechoic fluid collection surrounding the testis, distinct from normal testicular tissue
No internal vascularity or color flow within the fluid
Septations or low-level echoes within the fluid
No testicular mass or inguinal hernia

imaging.study: MRI scrotum without and with contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Rarely indicated; may be used if ultrasound is inconclusive or to further characterize a complex scrotal mass

findings.text: Simple hydrocele appears as non-enhancing fluid collection around the testis
May reveal an underlying testicular or paratesticular mass

confirmatory.why: Confirms a simple hydrocele and excludes testicular tumor, inguinal hernia, or other scrotal pathology

not_indicated.why: No role in uncomplicated hydrocele; complete blood count is typically normal.
Not indicated unless urinary tract symptoms are present.
Not indicated for simple hydrocele; obtained only if an underlying testicular mass is found on ultrasound.

decision_points: Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler is the test of choice when the diagnosis is uncertain or when an underlying testicular mass or torsion must be ruled out.
A hard, non-transilluminating scrotal mass requires urgent ultrasound and possibly serum tumor markers (AFP, beta-hCG, LDH).
In infants, congenital hydroceles often resolve by age 1; ultrasound is used only if the diagnosis is unclear or an associated hernia is suspected.

differential.name: Inguinal hernia
differential.why_considered: Scrotal swelling that may extend from the groin and change with activity
differential.trigger: Irreducible bulge with pain, nausea, or vomiting

history: Bulge increases with coughing, straining, or standing
Pain or discomfort in the groin
exam: Cough impulse felt over the swelling
imaging: Ultrasound shows bowel or omentum in the scrotum

differential.name: Testicular cancer
differential.why_considered: Painless scrotal swelling or a hard testicular mass
differential.trigger: Hard, non-transilluminating mass on the testis

history: Back pain or weight loss if metastatic
exam: May be associated with a hydrocele
labs: Elevated AFP, beta-hCG, or LDH in some cases
imaging: Ultrasound shows solid intratesticular mass with vascularity

exam: Relief of pain with elevation of the scrotum
imaging: Ultrasound shows enlarged, hypervascular epididymis or testis

differential.name: Varicocele
differential.why_considered: Scrotal swelling or dull ache, especially on the left

history: Dull ache that worsens with standing
imaging: Ultrasound shows dilated veins with increased flow on Valsalva

differential.name: Spermatocele
differential.why_considered: Painless scrotal mass separate from the testis

exam: Smooth cystic mass felt separately from the testis
imaging: Ultrasound shows anechoic cyst near the epididymal head

differential.name: Testicular torsion
differential.trigger: Sudden severe scrotal pain with nausea or vomiting

imaging: Ultrasound shows absent or reduced testicular Doppler flow

severity.mild: Small, asymptomatic hydrocele; no discomfort; testis easily palpable and transillumination positive
severity.moderate: Large hydrocele causing scrotal heaviness or dull ache; may limit physical activity; no acute signs
severity.severe: Very large, tense hydrocele causing significant discomfort, pressure, or difficulty with walking or clothing

red_flags.meaning: Underlying testicular cancer until proven otherwise

red_flags.finding: Acute severe scrotal pain with nausea or vomiting
Irreducible inguinal bulge with pain and vomiting
Fever, erythema, and tenderness of the scrotum
Rapidly enlarging scrotal swelling in an older adult
red_flags.meaning: May indicate an underlying testicular tumor

special_populations.differences: Congenital hydroceles usually resolve by age 1; observation is typical unless large, tense, or associated with an inguinal hernia.
Acquired hydroceles may hide an underlying testicular tumor; perform scrotal ultrasound before attributing the swelling to a simple hydrocele.

key_questions.question: When did you first notice the swelling, and how has it changed over time?
key_questions.looking_for: Insidious onset over weeks to months, or present since birth; slow enlargement

key_questions.question: Is the swelling on one side or both?
key_questions.looking_for: Usually unilateral; bilateral can occur in infants or communicating hydroceles

key_questions.question: Does the swelling change when you stand, strain, or lie down?
key_questions.looking_for: Communicating hydrocele may enlarge with standing/straining and decrease when recumbent

key_questions.question: Do you have any scrotal pain or discomfort?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent or only dull ache/heaviness; severe acute pain suggests torsion or strangulated hernia

key_questions.question: Any nausea or vomiting?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests bowel obstruction or strangulated hernia

key_questions.question: Any fever, chills, or scrotal redness and warmth?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests infection or epididymo-orchitis

key_questions.question: Any pain or burning with urination, penile discharge, or blood in the urine?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests epididymitis or urinary tract pathology

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent trauma to the scrotum or groin?
key_questions.looking_for: No trauma; trauma suggests hematocele or testicular injury

key_questions.question: Have you had any prior groin or scrotal surgery, hernia, or hydrocele?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior hernia or hydrocele repair; recurrence possible

key_questions.question: Have you ever had epididymitis, orchitis, or a sexually transmitted infection?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior infection may cause a reactive hydrocele

key_questions.question: Have you had sudden, severe scrotal pain with nausea or vomiting?
key_questions.looking_for: Rapidly excludes testicular torsion or strangulated hernia

reasoning_points: Insidious onset over weeks to months, or present since birth
No acute scrotal pain, fever, dysuria, or vomiting, making torsion, infection, and strangulated hernia less likely
No cough impulse, no reducible inguinal bulge, and no discrete testicular mass, helping exclude hernia and testicular tumor
Scrotal ultrasound may confirm an anechoic fluid collection with a normal testis and no internal flow
Congenital patent processus vaginalis considered in infants; reactive or idiopathic causes considered in adults

easy: Adult man with painless, unilateral, transilluminating scrotal swelling for months
Testis is palpable and normal, no cough impulse, no fever
Ultrasound confirms a simple anechoic hydrocele
Straightforward distinction from inguinal hernia by exam
medium: Infant with communicating hydrocele that changes size with crying and lying flat
Large hydrocele that obscures the testicle, making ultrasound necessary to exclude a mass
Adult with prior hernia repair and recurrent scrotal swelling, requiring distinction between recurrent hernia and hydrocele
Ultrasound shows a simple hydrocele but the underlying testis is not well seen
hard: Older adult with a hydrocele plus an underlying testicular tumor hidden by fluid
Tense or complex hydrocele with septations, debris, or calcifications, raising concern for infection or hematocele
Recent trauma with sudden scrotal enlargement, requiring distinction from hematocele and testicular rupture
Communicating hydrocele in an infant with an associated inguinal hernia at risk for incarceration
